question: Riddle time: I float on my back, smash shellfish open with a rock on my belly, and hold paws with my friends while I nap so we don't drift apart. What am I?
source_excerpt: When at the surface, it usually floats on its back and moves by sculling its feet and tail from side to side.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture a generic cute animal, then the clues narrow to one creature. The hand-holding detail is the line that makes them smile on the way to an answer they can reach.
extra.verification_notes: Sea otters float on their backs, pound shellfish on a rock held on the chest, and are documented holding paws while sleeping, which the question attributes to keeping groups together (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_otter).

explanation: Sea otters really do link paws while sleeping, and a resting group is called a raft. When no friend is around, they wrap themselves in kelp to stay anchored.

question: Fact or fiction: the wombat, an Australian marsupial, does its business in neat little cubes.
source_excerpt: Scientists have solved the mystery of how wombats poop cubes (paraphrased from the article title; the page was not opened)

extra.why_interesting: The claim sounds like an obvious made-up joke, so most players lean towards 'fiction'. It is real, it is well documented, and it even won an Ig Nobel Prize.
extra.verification_notes: Wombats produce cube-shaped droppings, formed in the intestine, per the Smithsonian (https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/scientists-have-solved-mystery-how-wombats-poop-cubes-180976898/); no newer finding contradicts this.

explanation: It's true. Uneven stretchiness in the last part of the wombat's gut moulds its droppings into cubes, which researchers explained in a study that won an Ig Nobel Prize. Flat sides probably help the droppings stay put on the rocks and logs wombats use as scent markers.

question: Crows in a Japanese city have recruited an unwitting helper to crack walnuts for them. What do they use?
source_excerpt: In Sendai, Japan, Carrion crows Corvus corone have frequently been observed to use automobiles as nutcrackers. Crows put walnuts in front of the wheels of automobiles

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a bird uses beaks or rocks. The answer, traffic, is something everyone sees daily, so it can be reasoned out and it delights once it clicks.
extra.verification_notes: Sendai carrion crows are documented placing walnuts before car wheels so cars crack them (Nihei, Tohoku Univ.); no newer development contradicts this.

explanation: The crows drop walnuts onto the road and let car tyres crush them. Some even wait for the traffic lights to stop the cars before hopping out to collect their snack.

question: What happens if you stand right behind a male hippo while it does its business?
alternative_answers: It spins its tail and flings dung
source_excerpt: muck-spreading, in which the tail is vigorously wagged during defecation. This action scatters feces in a wide range

extra.why_interesting: People think of hippos as dangerous at the front end. The comic surprise is that the rear end has its own propeller-powered weapon.
extra.verification_notes: Male hippos spin their tails while defecating, scattering dung over a wide area, so standing behind one gets you sprayed (Denver Zoo); females do this too, but that doesn't make the answer wrong.

explanation: A hippo whirls its short tail like a propeller while pooping and flings dung in every direction to mark its territory. Scientists actually call it dung showering.
